ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Sick Visit — Judy Garland — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for acute laryngitis

text.paragraph: Hoarse voice and sore throat for three days, during rehearsals. [S]

Ms. Garland asked for a same-day visit because her voice has been hoarse for three days. It began with a sore throat and a runny nose after several people in her rehearsal company had colds. Yesterday her voice cracked on high notes and today she can speak only quietly. She has a mild dry cough, worse at night, and felt warm yesterday. She has no trouble swallowing or breathing, no drooling, no neck swelling, and no heartburn. She has kept singing in rehearsals. She is taking phenobarbital 64.8 mg a day, and her next planned step down is due today. She asked for a steroid shot to get her voice back for rehearsals and for codeine cough syrup to help her sleep through the cough. She has taken no other medicine for it. [S]

list.item:
Acute laryngitis, probably viral (J04.0). Hoarseness of three days after a cold, without stridor, trouble swallowing, or signs of a bacterial infection. Hoarseness of less than four weeks after a cold does not need laryngoscopy unless it persists or there are warning signs. Antibiotics do not help. A steroid is not used routinely for acute laryngitis and was not given: it would not shorten a viral illness much, can affect mood and sleep during her taper, and should not be given without examining the vocal folds. [S]
Voice rest for three days, no singing until the voice returns, then a gradual return to singing; no whispering.
Fluids, humidified air and honey for the cough.
Acetaminophen 1,000 mg every 6 hours as needed, no more than 3,000 mg a day.
Laryngoscopy by an otolaryngologist if the hoarseness lasts four weeks, or sooner for stridor, trouble swallowing, coughing up blood or a high fever.

Barbiturate use disorder on a phenobarbital taper (F13.20). Codeine was not prescribed: an opioid added to phenobarbital deepens sedation and slows breathing, and dextromethorphan was also avoided while she is on a sedative. Because she is unwell, worried and sleeping poorly, today's planned step down is paused for two weeks, as the taper plan allows. Naloxone remains not indicated because no opioid has been prescribed. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm; the supply is in the locked box. [S]
Hold phenobarbital at 64.8 mg a day for two weeks; next step at the ten-week visit.
No codeine, dextromethorphan, antihistamine sleep aids or alcohol.
Her CBT-I routine continues; a cough at night is expected to settle within days.

Depression with anxiety on sertraline (F32.1). Worried about work; mood otherwise steady. [S]
Continue sertraline 50 mg daily.
A note to her company asking for three days off singing, with the reason given as a voice illness only, as she asked.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (2025); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); Clinical Practice Guideline: Hoarseness (Dysphonia) (Update) (2018)

Follow-up: Phone check in three days. Ten-week review in two weeks. Return sooner for trouble breathing or swallowing, or a high fever. Next scheduled visit 1955-08-31: ten-week review: phenobarbital taper, life after stopping the stimulant, sleep, mood, weight and work. [S]
